sentences.text: The subadult holotype specimen — the specific fossil the species is based on — is estimated to be around 13 meters long, while the larger paratype measures about 14 meters.
The holotype is identified as a subadult because its skull sutures have not yet fused, whereas the paratype displays fully fused sutures indicating it was an adult.
Its shoulder blade was strongly curved with a fan-shaped lower end, a feature unique among known sauropods.
The trunk consisted of 12 dorsal vertebrae and four sacral vertebrae.
Rod-like chevrons in the rear tail were closely attached to the centra and articulated at the mid-length of the vertebral centra, bracing the joint and restricting tail bending.
An adult specimen was found to contain radial fibrolamellar bone in the outermost layer of its humerus, a feature previously unreported in sauropods.
The presence of this rapid-growth bone tissue suggests the animal survived for some time after an injury caused accelerated bone growth.
Spinophorosaurus retained a non-reduced vestibular apparatus in its inner ear, which is unusual for heavy plant-eating quadrupeds.
Two specimens of Spinophorosaurus were excavated in the 2000s by German and Spanish teams working under difficult conditions.
The official excavation campaign, dubbed "Projekt Dino," started on March 1, 2007, traveling via Spain, Morocco, Mauritania, and Mali due to security risks in the Sahara.
The excavation of the first skeleton was completed on April 2, and the fossils were transported to the port of Cotonou on April 3.
Four theropod teeth were found near the holotype skeleton, three resembling Megalosauridae or Allosauridae and one possibly belonging to an early Spinosaurid.
Dinosaur tracks found near the site include a six-footprint trackway from a mid-sized sauropod and 120 two-toed theropod footprints.
Anatomical features such as a narrow snout, broad teeth, and a long humerus suggest Spinophorosaurus was adapted for high browsing.
One study suggests Spinophorosaurus may have been a high browser, while another examined possible mating postures.
In 2020, researchers revised the posture of Spinophorosaurus to be more vertical with high shoulders and an elevated neck, based on digital skeletal assembly.
A 2015 study using a 3D model found that the frontmost 20 tail vertebrae of Spinophorosaurus could deflect up to 20 degrees and sideways flex by 8 to 10 degrees.
Spinophorosaurus shares anatomical features with Middle Jurassic East Asian sauropods but differs significantly from those found in South America and India.
The animal possesses ancestral traits in East Asian sauropods that were previously thought to be derived features.
The genus Spinophorosaurus was named by Remes and colleagues in 2009.
Early studies classified Spinophorosaurus as one of the most primitive sauropods, closely related to Vulcanodon, Cetiosaurus, and Tazoudasaurus.
Many characteristics linking it to the African Tazoudasaurus present Spinophorosaurus as a typical basal sauropod of southern Gondwana.
The open postparietal notch on the skull rear margin is a feature shared with dicraeosaurids and Abrosaurus.
A 2022 study proposes that Spinophorosaurus is the most primitive member of the Mamenchisauridae group.
Spinophorosaurus is known from the Irhazer Shale, a geological formation thought to be of Middle Jurassic age.
Its stratigraphic and phylogenetic position suggests Spinophorosaurus lived during the Middle Jurassic, specifically the Bajocian to Bathonian stages.
It lived approximately 167 million years ago during the Bathonian stage of the Middle Jurassic in what is now Africa.
Spinophorosaurus likely lived across Asia and Africa during the late Early to Middle Jurassic periods.
During the Early and Middle Jurassic, the region where Spinophorosaurus lived was close to the equator with a summer-wet climate and high plant diversity.
It is debated whether the bones on the tail tip were spiked osteoderms or clavicles.
Researchers suggest that structures originally interpreted as tail spikes or osteoderms in Spinophorosaurus may actually be clavicles rather than armor.
Researchers suggest that geographic barriers separated the Middle Jurassic sauropod faunas of Laurasia and South Gondwana.
